newsitem.title: FRANCE: French, Russian ministers in talks on tsarist debt.
newsitem.headline: French, Russian ministers in talks on tsarist debt.

text.p: The prime ministers of Russia and France held talks on Tuesday in hopes of resolving a dispute over Moscow's tsarist debt that has blocked trade in a new Russian bond in France.

Prime Minister Alain Juppe intended to press the debt issue with his Russian counterpart Viktor Chernomyrdin during a Paris meeting of a commission on bilateral economic ties, French Finance and Foreign Trade Minister Yves Galland said.
However Galland warned French holders of the pre-revolutionary Russian bonds against building up unreasonable expectations for the talks.
"We cannot anticipate the results or speculate on the negotiations, which are taking place as we speak," Galland told the National Assembly during parliamentary questioning.

Chernomyrdin, in Paris for a two-day visit, said before leaving Moscow that Russia would pay the debt run up by its pre-1917 tsarist government and repudiated by the Soviet Union after the communist revolution.
The dispute marred Russia's return to international capital markets last week with an oversubscribed $1.0 billion Eurobond, its first debt offering since the 1917 revolution.

France banned trading in the Eurobond pending settlement of the compensation issue. The descendants of the original French buyers are claiming some 140 to 160 billion francs ($27 billion to $31 billion), mostly in unpaid interest.

The dispute is also seen as an obstacle to Russia joining the powerful Paris Club of government creditors, which France chairs, a move that would allow it to negotiate the return of Soviet-era debts owed to Moscow, mainly by developing countries.
Speculation about Chernomyrdin's intentions had prompted the Paris bourse to suspend trade in the pre-revolutionary bonds.
Officials in Moscow and Paris doubted there would be a final deal on Tuesday, saying negotiations were complex.

An estimated 1.2 million French investors bought Russian bonds issued up to 1917 to fund projects like the Trans-Siberian railway. The bond holders' association estimates that 400,000 people hold them today.
The Soviet refusal to meet the obligations of its tsarist predecessor left savers holding virtually worthless, if attractively printed, paper.
Moscow has settled smaller debt disputes with holders of the bonds in Britain, the United States, Canada and Switzerland.
Moscow has argued that any liability for Tsarist-era debt must be offset against the seizure in the West of Russian assets, which were used to help fight the Communists.

Chernomyrdin, who has been virtually running Russia while President Boris Yeltsin convalesces from heart bypass surgery on November 5, met conservative French President Jacques Chirac earlier on Tuesday.
Chirac spokeswoman Catherine Colonna said they had discussed the debt issue as well as Russia's continuing opposition to the eastward expansion of NATO.

She said Chirac reiterated his desire for a summit including NATO states, eastern European nations who wish to join it and former Soviet republics, including Russia, as a preliminary step toward an agreement between NATO and Moscow.
But Chernomyrdin responded that Moscow saw no reason at this time to alter its opposition to NATO expansion, Colonna said.
"We understand that Russia remains worried and convinced that enlargement would constitute a threat to Russia's security," Colonna said.
